prompt.problem_text: The Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP): one depot, identical vehicles of capacity Q, every customer visited exactly once by one vehicle, minimise the total distance; the number of routes is free. An instance file gives the capacity, two-dimensional integer coordinates of the depot (node 1) and the customers, and the customers' demands; a distance is the Euclidean distance rounded to the nearest integer. A solution file has one `Route #k: c1 c2 ...` line per route with customers numbered 1..n (customer i is node i+1 of the instance file), then `Cost <value>`.
prompt.solver_text: a hybrid genetic search for the CVRP, open-source C++, in `src/Program/`
prompt.time_text: 0.4 x n seconds of CPU time for an instance with n customers (40 s for n = 100, 400 s for n = 1000)
prompt.io_text: `solver <instance file> <solution file> -t <seconds> -seed <int> -round 1`; it must write the solution file and keep writing the search-progress file `<solution file>.PG.csv` (one line per new best solution)
prompt.class_text: CVRP with integer Euclidean coordinates, integer customer demands between 1 and the capacity, one depot, a free number of routes and no other constraint, with {lo} to {hi} customers
prompt.size_text: `--n` is the number of customers (the service asks for sizes across the public benchmark's range, {lo} to {hi}).

island_text:
This project is one of three that improve the same solver in parallel, all three on the same training instances. YOURS is the main one: your committed version is the one that will be tested at the end. The two others are scouts: they keep their own lines of versions, they are told to stay away from everything you have kept, dropped or are working on, and their role is to give you ideas you have not had. How it works for you:
- `offers/` receives every change a scout commits: one directory per offer, with `change.diff` (the change alone), `after/` (the changed files in full) and `note.md` (what it is and what it measured). The scouts work on the same instances as you, each on its own line of versions, so an offer's numbers are directly comparable with yours. Whatever you take from an offer goes through your own evaluations and your commit gate like any other change. Say in the evaluation note and in `NOTES.md` which offer it is (`offer S5_v2: ...`), what you decided and why.
- An offer usually needs further work from you before it pays off on your version. It was developed and tuned on the scout's own line of versions (often the original solver plus that one change), while your version contains other changes that interact with it: its parameters (rates, periods, sizes, thresholds), the place where it is applied and its share of the run time were chosen for another solver. So treat an offer as a starting point that you optimise, not as a patch that you accept or reject. When an offer does not pass as it is, adapt it to your version - re-tune its key parameters, change when or where it is applied, keep only the part that helps, combine it with what you already have - and measure again. Keep working on an offer until it pays off on your version, or until your measurements show why it cannot (for example: your version already does what it does, or a named interaction with one of your changes cancels it). Leaving an offer is the exception: `NOTES.md` must then give that reason, with every variant you tried and what each measured. A number of attempts is never a reason by itself, and one `probe` whose difference is within the noise is not a reason to leave an offer whose own measurement passed the gate. An offer that passes as it is can still be improved afterwards: look for that too. `offers/INDEX.md` (kept up to date by the service) lists the open offers with what you have measured on each so far and where the scout measured its effect (by instance size: test an offer on the instances it is meant for). Offers whose effect is established in the scout's project (they passed its first gate) are listed first: work on them in that order, before anything else - while one of them is open the service accepts no other declaration. Offers that passed there only through the second gate have an effect within the noise of the measurement: taking one of them up is your choice, and when none of the first group is open they compete for your time with your own ideas on their merits. An offer is closed by a commit of yours that contains it, or - when your measurements show why it cannot pay off on your version - by `python3 tools/ctl.py leave <offer> "<that reason, with the variants you measured>"`.
- `REF_*.md` are briefs of the scouts: what each tried without keeping (do not try it again: it was measured on your instances) and what it is working on now (do not duplicate it; it will arrive as an offer if it succeeds).
- Besides the offers, follow your own ideas.
- Before you start on a new direction (before you write code for it), declare it: `python3 tools/ctl.py claim "<one sentence>"`. The answer gives the record of the other two projects: what each is working on now, what it declared earlier, what it kept, and what it tried and did not keep. If yours is the same idea as anything on that record, or a variant of it, do not start it: think of another and declare that one. (An offer is the exception: it is yours to take up.) One declaration at a time (a new one replaces the old one). The service refuses `probe` and `eval` until you have declared a direction, and again after every commit until you declare the next one. An offer you take up is declared in the same way (`claim "offer S5_v2: ..."`).
